title: "Axolotl brain (Stereo-seq)"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", cache = TRUE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "/mnt/c/Users/tingthou/Desktop/SIGNAL/SingleCell/RealData")
```

This page analyses single-cell resolution Stereo-seq data of the axolotl brain
at developmental stage 57 (Wei *et al.*, 2022), with cell-type labels and the
panel of 11 spatial kernels. To keep the page quick, it runs three genes named
in the paper; the analysis of all 16,586 genes uses the same code and is best
split into batches on a cluster (below).

## Data

The processed data used on this page, `artista_data.RData`, can be downloaded
from the [SIGNAL real data folder](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1-j6l-KBT9dR_p2RB2RVb_5q9Ig2GdRn3)
on Google Drive. The raw data are in the ARTISTA database
(<https://db.cngb.org/stomics/artista/download/>); we removed mitochondrial
genes, kept genes with non-zero expression in at least 20 locations and
locations with non-zero expression for at least 20 genes.

```{r load}
library(SIGNAL)
library(Matrix)
load("artista_data.RData")
dim(data_use$count_use)
table(data_use$cluster)
```

## Step 1: create a SIGNAL object

Three genes from the paper: *AACS*, a cell-type gene; *TCF4*, a spatial gene;
and *SDC2*, a gene with a cell-type-specific spatial pattern.

```{r create}
genes <- c("AACS", "TCF4", "SDC2")
obj <- createSIGNALobject(data_use$count_use[genes, ], data_use$location_coord,
                          data_use$cluster)
obj
```

## Step 2: filter and transform

```{r preprocess}
obj <- SIGNAL_preprocess(obj, min_cells = 0, seed = 1)
```

## Step 3: build the kernels

Cell-type labels give the Hamming cell-type kernel. With 4,410 cells (fewer
than 6,000), SIGNAL builds the panel of 11 spatial kernels.

```{r kernel}
obj <- SIGNAL_kernel(obj)
names(obj@spatial_kernels)
```

## Step 4: test the genes

```{r test}
obj <- SIGNAL_test(obj, ncores = 3, verbose = FALSE)
signif(obj@result, 3)
```

```{r classify}
res <- obj@result
apply(res[, c("p_celltype", "p_spatial", "p_ctSVG")] < 0.05, 1, function(f)
  paste(c("CellType", "Spatial", "ctSVG")[f], collapse = "+"))
```

Values of about 1e-16 are below the accuracy of Davies' method (about 1e-6);
use `method = "saddlepoint"` to keep their actual size.

## Step 5: visualise the genes

```{r plot-aacs}
SIGNAL_plotGene(obj, "AACS", by_celltype = TRUE, point_size = 0.5)
```

```{r plot-tcf4}
SIGNAL_plotGene(obj, "TCF4", by_celltype = TRUE, point_size = 0.5)
```

```{r plot-sdc2}
SIGNAL_plotGene(obj, "SDC2", by_celltype = TRUE, point_size = 0.5)
```

## Step 6: cell types behind the cell-type-specific pattern

```{r celltype}
obj <- SIGNAL_celltype(obj, genes = "SDC2", ncores = 3, verbose = FALSE)
signif(obj@celltype_result, 2)
```

## All genes: batches on a cluster

The genes are tested independently, so the 16,586 genes can be split over the
tasks of a Slurm job array, and the result tables combined afterwards:

```{r batches, eval = FALSE}
part  <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID"))
genes <- rownames(data_use$count_use)
batch <- genes[parallel::splitIndices(length(genes), 100)[[part]]]
obj <- SIGNAL(data_use$count_use[batch, ], data_use$location_coord, data_use$cluster,
              min_cells = 0, seed = 1)            # ncores = the Slurm allocation
saveRDS(obj@result, sprintf("artista_part_%03d.rds", part))
```

```{bash, eval = FALSE}
sbatch --array=1-100 --cpus-per-task=20 --mem-per-cpu=4G --time=24:00:00 run_artista.sh
```

With 4,410 cells, each spatial kernel takes about 17 minutes for 160 genes on
20 cores, so a batch of 160 genes needs about 3 hours and 30 GB of memory.
